title: Week 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Motivation
Overview. This lecture begins by comparing traditional software, which is generally rule-based; machine learning, which learns patterns and behavior from data; and deep learning, a branch of machine learning that focuses on training neural networks. We then build up two linear models, linear regression and logistic regression, that serve as building blocks for everything else in this course. Specifically, we introduce linear models from the perspective of deep learning in order to present the core concepts of loss functions, gradient descent, and the chain rule for differentiation.

title: Week 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Rule-based software
Consider the task of classifying handwritten images as 0 or 1. This task is simple enough that it can mostly be solved with a simple heuristic rule: a 0 almost always has at least two dark pixels crossing its middle row whereas a 1 has just one. This can be hard-coded by hand, producing something like the following:
n_dark = 0
for pixel in middle_row:
    # Assume pixel values range from 0-255
    if pixel < 100:
        n_dark += 1
if n_dark > 1:
    return 0
else:
    return 1
This simple program might work acceptably well for 0 vs 1 classification, but what about classifying all ten handwritten digits? One could start by trying to enumerate different heuristic rules to distinguish the digits, but the wide range of writing styles and possible digit positions and shapes quickly makes a rule-based system intractable. More complex problems–even those that we might consider “simple” like classifying an image as being a picture of a cat or dog–are clearly out of reach.


Machine learning
How can we design computer programs for problems that are too complex to allow for simply writing down a set of rules? In this case, while we might not be able to come up with a rule set, we may be able to come up with a training set, i.e. a collection of inputs and the corresponding desired output for the program.

Definition. Machine learning produces programs whose behavior is learned from data rather than hand-coded. Given examples of desired input–output pairs, machine learning aims to automatically adjust the program to better reproduce the function underlying the input-output mapping.

After collecting a training dataset, the first step in old-fashioned machine learning is to design a set of features. Features are computable measurements about the input (e.g., the number of dark pixels per row or the presence of a certain stroke pattern). We typically represent the input feature values as a feature vector \bm{x} by assembling all feature measurements for a given input into a fixed-length vector. In old-fashioned machine learning, these features are generally used with simple models, i.e. models that are constrained to have a simple structure that makes them amenable to optimization. The use of a simple model makes the success of old-fashioned ML depend heavily on the quality of hand-designed features. Designing the best feature for complex tasks like large-scale object recognition across tens of thousands of categories is challenging, and feature engineering can become the limiting factor in model performance.

Deep learning
What should we do to overcome the limits of feature engineering? Deep learning asks: If we are learning the model, why not learn the features too? In other words, instead of hand-designing features based on intuition and experimentation, perhaps we can directly learn features that are well-suited to the training data. As long as we have sufficient data and can effectively train such models, we might naturally expect this approach to work better. Indeed, since the resurgence of this basic idea in the early 2000s, deep learning has enabled a dizzying array of breakthroughs and transformative technologies.

Definition. Deep learning studies models that are big, complex, differentiable functions built by composing many small, simple, differentiable functions called layers. Because the full composition is differentiable, the parameters of every layer can be trained jointly, end-to-end, with gradient descent.

text:
Why Deep Learning Was Hard
The core techniques underlying deep learning, such as neural networks and gradient descent, have existed since the 1950s. If deep learning is so powerful, why wasn’t it the prevalent approach to machine learning until recently? For old-fashioned ML with fixed features and a simple classifier, the training loss is often convex as a function of the parameters. This means that, under benign assumptions, gradient descent is guaranteed to find the minimum, and we can be reasonably confident that the solution generalizes well to unseen data. In deep learning, we have no such guarantees. In practice, the loss is highly non-convex, and can be riddled with local optima, saddle points, and flat regions. As a result, small errors in training can lead to large errors at test time.

title: Week 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Linear Regression
For the rest of this lecture we study two foundational linear models.

Definition. Linear regression is a model that predicts a scalar value from an input feature vector. The prediction is an affine function of the features, meaning that any change in a feature always produces a constant, proportional change in the output.

As a running example, consider the task of predicting a home’s sale price from three features: its age (years), the square footage (sqft), and the number of bedrooms (nbr).
\hat{y} = w_1 \cdot \text{age} + w_2 \cdot \text{sqft} + w_3 \cdot \text{nbr} + b
where w_1, w_2, and w_3 are the weights assigned to each feature value and \hat{y} is the predicted price. The features can be combined into a feature vector \bm{x} = [\text{age},\, \text{sqft},\, \text{nbr}]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3 and weights into the weight vector \bm{w} = [w_1, w_2, w_3]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^3, giving the standard expression for a linear regression model:
\hat{y} = \bm{w}^\top \bm{x} + b
The weight vector \bm{w} and bias value b are the parameters of the model. Together we write them as the parameter vector \bm{\theta} = (\bm{w}, b). In general, the parameters \bm{\theta} of a given model are the values that are tuned via optimization and “learned” from data.
What if we want to process more than one example at a time? As we will discuss later, this is common during both training and inference, or “test time”, when the trained model is being used to make predictions. We can assemble N feature vectors into a matrix \bm{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} and compute the model’s predictions as
\hat{\bm{y}} = \bm{X}\bm{w} + b, \qquad \hat{\bm{y}} \in \mathbb{R}^N, \quad \bm{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d}

The loss function
Given a model, we need a way to tune the parameters to fit the data. To determine how well the model fits the data (and ultimately as an objective to be optimized), we use a loss function. For regression (predicting a scalar value) a common loss function is the squared error loss:
\mathcal{L}(\hat{y}, y) = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{y} - y)^2
where y is the true label for the input \bm{x} used to produce the prediction \hat{y}. The \frac{1}{2} is included for convenience because it will cancel out the exponent of 2 when we differentiate. The goal is to find \bm{\theta} that minimizes \mathcal{L} over the training set.






Note



In the past, you may have fit linear regression via the closed-form solution \bm{w}^* = (\bm{X}^\top \bm{X})^{-1}\bm{X}^\top \bm{y} that arises when analytically finding the minimum of the loss function. In this course, we ignore the closed-form solution and instead use gradient descent because it generalizes to neural networks whereas a closed-form solution does not.




Gradient descent
Gradient descent is the core optimization algorithm used in deep learning. Gradient descent is an iterative algorithm where, at each step, we move the parameters in the direction that most rapidly decreases the loss. As long as the function being optimized is not too complex and as long as we don’t move too much, we can be confident that we’ve decreased the loss. If we do this over and over again, we might hope to reach a minimum of the function.

Gradient Descent
Initialize parameters \bm{\theta} (we will discuss how to do this later!).
Repeat until a stopping criterion is met: \bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \eta\,\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}
where \eta > 0 is the learning rate and \nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L} is the gradient of the loss with respect to \bm{\theta}.

There are many ways to decide when to stop performing gradient descent. Since loss functions are generally nonnegative, a natural criterion is to wait until the loss reaches zero, but this is only possible if the model can perfectly fit the data. In the case of a linear model, this would mean that the input-output relationship is perfectly linear, which is rarely the case. Other heuristics used as stopping criteria include:

The loss stops decreasing, or its rate of decrease gets sufficiently slow.
Performance on held-out validation data stops improving.
We run out of compute budget or patience.

Apart from the stopping criteria, to use gradient descent we must also specify a learning rate. Broadly, the learning rate dictates how quickly optimization progresses. However, as mentioned above (and as we will discuss further later), the gradient at a given location is only a local property of the function. Too large of a learning rate can therefore prevent gradient descent from making reliable progress and can even cause divergence, where the loss increases. Overall, we strive for a “just right” learning rate where the loss steadily decreases.

Computing the gradients: the chain rule
Performing gradient descent requires \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}, or in the case of linear regression, \nabla_{\bm{w}}\mathcal{L} and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b}. For a differentiable model, we can compute these conveniently by applying the chain rule, which treats \mathcal{L} as a composition of functions.
For example, when computing the loss of a single training example (\bm{x}, y) using linear regression, we have
\hat{y} = \bm{w}^\top \bm{x} + b, \qquad \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat{y} - y)^2
If we consider \mathcal{L} as a function of \hat{y} and \hat{y} as a function of \bm{w} (or b) and apply the chain rule, we have

\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\bm{w}} &= \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\hat{y}} \cdot \frac{d\hat{y}}{d\bm{w}}, \\
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{db} &= \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\hat{y}} \cdot \frac{d\hat{y}}{db}
\end{aligned}

We can compute these derivatives individually as 
\begin{aligned}
\dfrac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\hat{y}} &= \hat{y} - y, \qquad \dfrac{d\hat{y}}{d\bm{w}} = \bm{x}, \\
\dfrac{d\hat{y}}{db} &= 1
\end{aligned}

Substituting in these individual derivatives, we have
\nabla_{\bm{w}}\mathcal{L} = (\hat{y} - y)\,\bm{x}, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b} = \hat{y} - y
For linear regression, the gradient has a clean interpretation: the update for weight w_i is the prediction error (\hat{y} - y) scaled by the feature value x_i. In this way, features that appear more strongly in the input receive proportionally larger weight updates.


Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent
So far, we have computed the gradient of the loss for a single example. In practice it is common to compute the gradient for more than one example and update the parameters using the average gradient, like so:
\bm{\theta} \leftarrow \bm{\theta} - \frac{\eta}{B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \nabla_{\bm{\theta}} \mathcal{L}^{(i)}
where B is called the batch size. In the most extreme case, we could set the batch size equal to our training set size and compute the average gradient of all of the examples in our training set. However, computing the gradient for every example at every step of training might be unnecessarily expensive, as we will discuss later. More common in deep learning is therefore to draw a random sample of B examples from the training set at each iteration.


Hyperparameters
Unlike parameters like \bm{w} and b, hyperparameters are generally not learned from data but instead are set by the practitioner, typically through trial and error or heuristics. So far we have observed the following hyperparameters:



Hyperparameter
Description




\eta (learning rate)
Step size per gradient update


Batch size B
Number of examples per gradient update


Stopping criterion
When to stop training


Initialization scheme
Starting values for \bm{w} and b



We will revisit all of these as the course progresses.

title: Week 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Softmax (Logistic) Regression
The goal of regression is to produce a continuous scalar value. However, many problems of interest involve assigning the input a discrete label from a set of possible class labels. Such problems are referred to classification tasks.
Labels are further distinguished by the fact that, unlike the continuous values predicted during regression, they generally are unordered. For example, there is a natural order to the value of a house because a price of $213,000 is more than $190,000. In contrast, if we are predicting whether an image contains a picture of a cat or a dog, it would not be valid to say “cat is greater than dog” (or vice versa).
To turn our running “home price prediction” example into a classification task, we could instead aim to predict whether a given home would sell above asking, below asking, or not sell. In this way, it becomes a 3-class classification problem. As before, we will aim to make this prediction from its age, square footage, number of bedrooms, and asking price.

One-hot encoding
Representing class labels as integer class IDs (e.g. 1, 2, 3) would imply some kind of ordering. We instead represent class labels as one-hot vectors, which are length-K (where K is the number of classes) vectors with a 1 at the position of the correct class and 0s elsewhere. In the home price example, we would use the following three one-hot vectors for our classes:

\begin{aligned}
\text{“below asking”} &\;\to\; \bm{y} = [1,\, 0,\, 0]^\top \\
\text{“above asking”} &\;\to\; \bm{y} = [0,\, 1,\, 0]^\top \\
\text{“not sold”} &\;\to\; \bm{y} = [0,\, 0,\, 1]^\top
\end{aligned}

Note that the (Euclidean) distance between any two distinct one-hot vectors is always \sqrt{2}, thereby implying no order of any kind. As we will see later, one-hot vectors can also be interpreted as a probability distribution, where a given example’s assigned class is given a probability of 1 and the remaining classes have probability 0.


From scores to probabilities
To make a prediction, a softmax regression model first computes a score o_j for each class via a linear transformation of the features:
\bm{o} = \bm{W}\bm{x} + \bm{b}, \qquad \bm{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d},\;\; \bm{b} \in \mathbb{R}^K,\;\; \bm{o} \in \mathbb{R}^K
For the running example (K=3, d=4), \bm{W} has 3 \times 4 = 12 entries and \bm{b} has 3, so the model has 15 parameters in all. A larger score means the model considers that class more likely. Note that each of these scores are produced in essentially the same way as the scalar output of a linear regression model. To convert the set of predicted scores to a valid probability distribution (non-negative, summing to 1), we apply the softmax function:
\operatorname{softmax}(\bm{o})_j = \frac{\exp(o_j)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(o_k)}
Since \exp(o_j) \geq 0 for all j, the output values of softmax are non-negative. Additionally, we have that
\sum_j \operatorname{softmax}(\bm{o})_j = \frac{\displaystyle \sum_{j = 1}^K \exp(o_j)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(o_k)} = 1
Consequently, the output of the softmax function forms a valid probability distribution. We therefore can write the full softmax regression model as
P(y \mid \bm{x}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\bm{W}\bm{x} + \bm{b})
Effectively, as a given class’ score becomes higher, the model assigns a higher probability to that class and a lower probability to the other classes.

Softmax Explorer

}

title: Week 1: Introduction, Linear & Logistic Regression
text:
Cross-Entropy Loss
For linear regression, we used a squared error loss. While it is technically possible to use a squared error loss to train a softmax regression model, in practice it is much more common to use the cross-entropy loss.1

From maximum likelihood to cross-entropy
Recall that we can consider softmax regression as producing a probability distribution over classes conditioned on the input. A natural objective would therefore be to maximize the model’s assigned probability to the true class over a dataset of labeled examples. Concretely, given N training examples \{(\bm{x}^{(i)}, \bm{y}^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^N, we can start by aiming to maximize the joint likelihood:
\max_{\bm{\theta}} \prod_{i=1}^{N} P_{\bm{\theta}}(y^{(i)} \mid \bm{x}^{(i)})
It’s typical to maximize the log likelihood instead, because the logarithm is a monotonic function (so the parameter values corresponding to the maximum don’t change when you apply it) and because a product of probabilities can cause underflow and other numerical instabilities. Additionally, in machine learning we generally minimize a loss rather than maximize an objective. This leads to the minimization of the negative log-likelihood:
\min_{\bm{\theta}} -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \log P_{\bm{\theta}}(y^{(i)} \mid \bm{x}^{(i)})
We can write this in the following equivalent form:
\min_{\bm{\theta}} -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{K} \bm{y}_j^{(i)} \log P_{\bm{\theta}}(y^{(i)} \mid \bm{x}^{(i)})
by noting that \bm{y}^{(i)} is one-hot. This final equation is the cross-entropy loss, a quantity from information theory that measures how “wrong” a probability distribution is relative to the ground truth.
We can express the cross-entropy loss for a single example using the softmax regression model with scores \bm{o} = \bm{W}\bm{x} + \bm{b} and one-hot label \bm{y} as

\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}(\bm{y}, \hat{\bm{y}}) &= -\sum_j y_j \log \frac{\exp(o_j)}{\sum_k \exp(o_k)} \\
&= \sum_j y_j \log \sum_k \exp(o_k) - \sum_j y_j o_j \\
&= \log \sum_k \exp(o_k) \;-\; \sum_j y_j o_j
\end{aligned}

where the simplifications come from the quotient rule of the logarithm and the fact that \sum_j y_j = 1. To perform gradient descent, we only need one additional term compared to those used in linear regression: \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{do_j}. The reexpression above makes \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{do_j} straightforward to derive:

\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{do_j} &= \frac{d}{do_j}\!\left[\log \sum_k \exp(o_k)\right] - y_j \\
& = \frac{\exp(o_j)}{\sum_k \exp(o_k)} - y_j \\
&= \operatorname{softmax}(\bm{o})_j - y_j \\
&= \hat{y}_j - y_j
\end{aligned}

which can be expressed in vector form as \nabla_{\bm{o}} \mathcal{L} = \hat{\bm{y}} - \bm{y}. Intuitively, the gradient of the cross-entropy loss for the softmax regression model is simply the gap between the predicted probability and the ground-truth label. When the model assigns all of its probability to the correct label, the gradient is zero; but as the model becomes more incorrect, the gradient increases.

Limitations of Linear Models
Recap. Recall from Lecture 1 that both linear regression and logistic regression are considered linear models. In this lecture, we first discuss the limitations of linear models. Then, we introduce multi-layer perceptrons as our first non-linear model. To train multi-layer perceptrons, we introduce the full backpropagation algorithm. We conclude with a discussion of how multi-layer perceptrons can represent any function.
More precisely, a linear model satisfies the following two properties:

title: Week 2: Multi-Layer Perceptrons & Backpropagation
text:
Definition. A model \hat{y} = wx + b is a linear model if an increase or decrease in any feature must always increase or decrease the output by the same proportional amount, regardless of the current value of x.



Monotonicity. If w > 0, then x \uparrow \Rightarrow \hat{y} \uparrow always (and vice versa for w < 0).
Constant effect. The rate of change \dfrac{\partial\hat{y}}{\partial x} = w is the same everywhere. Informally, the graph of \hat{y} vs x is a straight line.


When linearity fails
Some relationships are approximately linear. For instance, larger houses tend to cost more, and a linear fit could be a reasonable approximation of this relationship. But many interesting problems involve nonlinearities. Consider the relationship between the number of doctor visits per year and the patient’s age: visits are very frequent in infancy, drop through young adulthood, then climb again in old age. This U-shaped curve is neither monotonic nor linear.






Linear: As house size increases, price rises monotonically when other factors remain unchanged; a linear model captures this perfectly.







Non-linear: doctor visits follow a U-shaped curve over age; no linear model can represent this.





While nonlinearity can sometimes be dealt with via feature engineering (e.g. taking the log of a feature with an exponential relationship in order to enable use of a linear model), deep learning aims to avoid feature engineering and instead learn the relationship “from scratch”.

text:
The Multi-Layer Perceptron
Remember, the central idea in deep learning is to build complex models that can model complex relationships by composing many simple, differentiable functions.

Why stacking linear layers doesn’t help
We have already seen one example of a layer in this class: The linear layer underlying linear and logistic regression. Given that we’ve already been exposed to linear layers, let’s try composing two of them:
H = XW_1, \qquad O = HW_2
Substituting, we get O = X\underbrace{W_1 W_2}_{=:\,W}. The product of two matrices is another matrix, so O = XW can still be considered a linear model.






Warning



Key fact. Composing linear (affine) transformations always yields another linear transformation. No matter how many linear layers you stack, the composition is equivalent to a single affine map. Depth adds no expressive power without nonlinearity.




Adding nonlinearity
The fix: insert a nonlinear function \sigma (the activation function or nonlinearity) between the linear layers:
\boxed{H = \sigma(XW_1 + b_1), \qquad O = HW_2 + b_2}
Because \sigma is nonlinear, O is now a nonlinear function of X.
Element-wise application. Inside neural networks \sigma is applied element-wise:
h_i = \sigma(x_i)
Each output element depends on exactly one input element (\sigma is a scalar function of a scalar) replicated independently at every position. This is in contrast to softmax (from Lecture 1), where every output depends on all inputs.

The architecture above is a two-layer fully-connected multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Every input is connected to every hidden unit, and every hidden unit to every output, hence fully connected. The names for this architecture:

text:
Backpropagation
Let \mathcal{L} denote the loss function, a scalar that measures the discrepancy between the model’s predictions and the true targets. Training proceeds by minimizing \mathcal{L} using gradient descent, which requires computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter in the model, i.e., \dfrac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} for each weight matrix W^m.
Backpropagation provides an algorithm for evaluating all such gradients by systematically applying the chain rule of calculus from the output layer back to the input layer. It can achieve more efficiency by reusing intermediate quantities computed during the forward pass, avoiding redundant calculations and enabling gradient computation in time proportional to a single forward evaluation.

The Chain Rule: Two Cases
Case 1: single intermediate variable. If \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}(z(w)):
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw} = \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dz}\,\frac{dz}{dw}
Case 2: multiple intermediate variables. If \mathcal{L} reaches w through z_1(w), z_2(w), \ldots, z_N(w) independently, i.e. \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}(z_1(w), z_2(w), \ldots, z_N(w)):
\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dw} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_i}\,\frac{dz_i}{dw}
Think of it as: sum the derivative contribution along every path from w to \mathcal{L}. Both cases come up repeatedly in the backprop derivation.


Notation and Definitions
For an L-layer MLP:








Symbol
Meaning
Shape




L
Number of layers
scalar (integer)


N^m
Width (# units) of layer m
scalar (integer)


W^m
Weight matrix for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m \times N^{m-1}}


b^m
Bias vector for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m}


\sigma^m
Nonlinearity at layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m} \to \mathbb{R}^{N^m} (element-wise)


a^m
Pre-activations for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m}


h^m
Activations for layer m
\mathbb{R}^{N^m}


h^0
Model input \mathbf{x}
\mathbb{R}^{N^0}


y
Target output
\mathbb{R}^{N^L}


\mathcal{L}
Loss: \mathcal{L}(h^L,\, y) \in \mathbb{R}
scalar (real number)



The forward pass computes, for m = 1, \ldots, L:
a^m = W^m h^{m-1} + b^m \qquad (\text{pre-activations}) h^m = \sigma^m(a^m) \qquad (\text{activations})
Backprop requires two quantities pre-specified from the model design:

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L}: derivative of the loss w.r.t. the model output (e.g. cross-entropy gradient).
\frac{dh^m}{da^m} = (\sigma^m)'(a^m): derivative of the nonlinearity (sigmoid, ReLU, etc.), computed in Activation Functions.



Deriving the Weight Gradient
We want \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m_{ij}} for any entry (i,j), where i \in \{1,\ldots,N^m\} indexes the unit in layer m (row) and j \in \{1,\ldots,N^{m-1}\} indexes the unit in layer m-1 (column). In other words, W^m_{ij} is the weight of the connection from unit j in layer m-1 to unit i in layer m.
Step 1: Apply the chain rule, pivoting through a^m.
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m_{ij}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N^m} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m_k} \frac{\partial a^m_k}{\partial W^m_{ij}}
Step 2: Evaluate \partial a^m_k / \partial W^m_{ij}.
Expanding a^m_k explicitly: a^m_k = \sum_{\ell=1}^{N^{m-1}} W^m_{k\ell}\,h^{m-1}_\ell + b^m_k.
The weight W^m_{ij} appears only in the formula for a^m_i (the i-th row). Therefore:
\frac{\partial a^m_k}{\partial W^m_{ij}} = \begin{cases} h^{m-1}_j & k = i \\ 0 & k \neq i \end{cases}
Here i and j are fixed: they name the one weight we are differentiating. i is its row, the unit in layer m that the weight feeds into, and j is its column, the unit in layer m-1 that the weight reads from. The index k runs over all units in layer m, k = 1, \ldots, N^m, asking whether the k-th pre-activation depends on this weight. The formula for a^m_k uses only row k of W^m, so the weight in row i can affect a^m_k only when k = i. In that case the weight multiplies h^{m-1}_j (the \ell = j term of the sum), which is the derivative. For every other k, row i never appears, so the derivative is 0.






TipQuestion: How do W and a interact in the forward pass, and why does that make the derivative nonzero only when k equals i?





Start from the dimensions. W^m has shape N^m \times N^{m-1}: one row per unit in layer m, one column per unit in layer m-1. The pre-activation a^m is a vector of length N^m: one entry per unit in layer m. So the number of rows of W^m equals the number of entries of a^m.
That match is not a coincidence. The forward pass pairs them one to one. Row i of W^m has N^{m-1} entries, one per unit in layer m-1, and it is combined with the previous activations h^{m-1} (also length N^{m-1}) in a dot product, plus the bias, to produce the single number a^m_i:
a^m_i = \sum_{\ell=1}^{N^{m-1}} W^m_{i\ell}\, h^{m-1}_\ell + b^m_i
No other row of W^m enters this sum. Reading the derivative \frac{\partial a^m_k}{\partial W^m_{ij}} as “if we nudge this one weight, how much does a^m_k move?”, a weight in row i can only move the entry that row i produces, which is a^m_i. So the nonzero case is k = i, and it is h^{m-1}_j because the weight in column j multiplies the j-th previous activation.
For example, in the worked example below, W^1 is 2 \times 2, h^0 = (1, 2)^\top, and b^1 = (0, -0.5)^\top. Take the weight W^1_{21} = -1 (i = 2, j = 1). The two pre-activations are
a^1_1 = 1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 = 3 \qquad a^1_2 = W^1_{21} \cdot 1 + 0.5 \cdot 2 - 0.5 = -0.5
Nudging W^1_{21} by \varepsilon changes a^1_2 to -0.5 + \varepsilon, so \frac{\partial a^1_2}{\partial W^1_{21}} = 1 = h^0_1 (the case k = i). It leaves a^1_1 = 3 unchanged, so \frac{\partial a^1_1}{\partial W^1_{21}} = 0 (the case k \neq i). This is also why the sum over k in Step 1 collapses to a single term.



Step 3: Collapse the sum. All terms except k=i are zero:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m_{ij}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m_i} \cdot h^{m-1}_j
Step 4: Matrix form. The vector \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} has shape N^m and h^{m-1} has shape N^{m-1}. Their outer product gives the gradient matrix of shape N^m \times N^{m-1}, matching W^m:

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} \cdot (h^{m-1})^\top







TipQuestion: The weight gradient uses the previous layer’s activations. What do we use at the first layer, where there is no earlier layer?





The formula asks for h^{m-1}, and at m = 1 that is h^0. The notation table defines h^0 as the model input \mathbf{x}, so the first layer has a previous “layer” after all: the data itself. The forward pass already relies on this, since a^1 = W^1 h^0 + b^1. The weight gradient for layer 1 is therefore
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^1} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1}\, \mathbf{x}^\top
This is why the forward pass caches the input as well as the hidden activations: \mathbf{x} plays the same role for W^1 that h^1 plays for W^2.
Backpropagation also stops at a^1. We never compute \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^0}, because the input is data and not a parameter we update.
In the worked example below, the first example has \mathbf{x} = (1, 2)^\top and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1} = (0.25, 0)^\top (its column of the batch gradient). Its contribution to \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^1} is the outer product
\begin{pmatrix} 0.25 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.25 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
and the batch gradient adds the second example’s contribution in the same way.



The bias gradient follows the same derivation and is simpler: differentiating a^m_i with respect to b^m_i gives 1 rather than h^{m-1}_j, so \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b^m} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m}.


The Backward Recursion
We still need \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m}. This is where the “back” in backprop comes from.
Base case (m = L):
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} \odot \frac{dh^L}{da^L}
Both factors are pre-specified. \odot is element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication.






TipQuestion: Why is the activation derivative combined with an elementwise product here, when the chain rule uses matrix products elsewhere?





In the base case, \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} \odot \frac{dh^L}{da^L} multiplies by the activation’s derivative one entry at a time, and the recursion below does the same at every hidden layer. This is still the chain rule.
The chain rule for vectors always multiplies by a Jacobian matrix, the matrix of partial derivatives of a layer’s outputs with respect to its inputs. The elementwise (Hadamard) product is that same matrix product in the special case where the Jacobian is a diagonal matrix:
\operatorname{diag}(d)\,v = d \odot v
So \odot is the diagonal matrix product written without building an N^m \times N^m matrix. A diagonal matrix equals its own transpose, so no transpose appears on that factor. Which case we are in depends on how each output depends on the inputs:








Dependence
Jacobian
Chain-rule step




One scalar in, one scalar out
a number
ordinary multiplication


Each output depends only on the input in the same position (elementwise, like \sigma)
diagonal
Hadamard product \odot


Every output depends on every input (like a linear layer)
dense
matrix product with the transpose



Example. Take the incoming gradient g = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^1} = (0.25, -0.5)^\top at a hidden layer with pre-activations a^1 = (3, -0.5)^\top and h^1 = \operatorname{ReLU}(a^1) = (3, 0)^\top. These are the numbers for the first example in the worked example below. We want \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1}.
First build the Jacobian entry by entry. Since h^1_1 = \operatorname{ReLU}(a^1_1) does not contain a^1_2, we get \frac{\partial h^1_1}{\partial a^1_2} = 0, and likewise \frac{\partial h^1_2}{\partial a^1_1} = 0. The diagonal entries are the ReLU slopes, 1 at a^1_1 = 3 and 0 at a^1_2 = -0.5:
\frac{\partial h^1}{\partial a^1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
The chain rule sums over both hidden units, and the zero off-diagonal entries kill the cross terms:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1_1} = \underbrace{0.25 \cdot 1}_{\text{through } h^1_1} + (-0.5) \cdot 0 = 0.25
The first term goes through h^1_1 and the second through h^1_2, which contributes nothing.
In matrix form this is the product with the diagonal Jacobian, which matches the Hadamard product:
\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0.25 \\ -0.5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.25 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 0.25 \\ -0.5 \end{pmatrix} \odot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.25 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
Now compare the linear step that produced g. With W^2 = (0.5, -1) and \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^2} = 0.5, the single output a^2 = 0.5\,h^1_1 - 1\,h^1_2 + 0.5 depends on both hidden units, so its Jacobian W^2 has no zeros and both terms of the sum survive:
g = {W^2}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^2} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot 0.5 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.25 \\ -0.5 \end{pmatrix}
This is the same “collapse the sum” idea as in the weight-gradient derivation. It collapses to one term when each output depends on one input, which is why \odot works, and it does not collapse when every output depends on every input, which is why the weights need a real matrix product. Softmax from Lecture 1 falls in the dense case, so its backward step needs a full matrix product.



Recursive case (m < L): Expanding via the chain rule, pivoting through the next layer’s pre-activations a^{m+1}:
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m_k} &= \left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{N^{m+1}} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}_\ell} \cdot W^{m+1}_{\ell k}\right) \\
&\quad \cdot \frac{dh^m_k}{da^m_k}
\end{aligned}
In matrix form:

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} = \left({W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}\right) \odot \frac{dh^m}{da^m}







TipQuestion: The recursion needs the gradient from layer m+1. What do we use at the last layer, where there is no next layer?





The recursion pulls the gradient backward through the weights of the next layer, {W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}. At m = L there is no W^{L+1} and no a^{L+1}, so nothing is passed back from a later layer. That is why the algorithm has a separate base case, and why the recursion is stated only for m < L.
At the last layer the signal comes straight from the loss. The model output h^L is the argument of \mathcal{L}(h^L, y), so \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} is found by differentiating the loss formula directly. The chain rule then needs one more link, from h^L back to a^L, and that link is the same elementwise activation derivative used in every hidden layer:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} \odot \frac{dh^L}{da^L}
Both factors are known from the model design, which is why the notes list them as “pre-specified”. In the worked example below, the output layer is the identity and the loss is \tfrac{1}{2}(h^2 - y)^2. For the first example alone, h^2 = 2 and y = 1, so \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^2} = h^2 - y = 1, \frac{dh^2}{da^2} = 1, and therefore \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^2} = 1. (The worked example averages over a batch of two, so its value is 0.5.) From here the recursion takes over: layer 1’s gradient is built from this number.



The key observation: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} depends on \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}; the gradient one layer forward. Starting from m=L and going backwards, each step feeds the next. This is backpropagation.
Summarized as a clean algorithm:

Backpropagation Algorithm
Pre-specify (from model design):

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L}: loss gradient w.r.t. the model output.
\frac{dh^m}{da^m} = (\sigma^m)'(a^m): nonlinearity derivative at each layer.

Forward pass: compute and cache all activations: h^0 = \mathbf{x}, \quad a^m = W^m h^{m-1} + b^m, \quad h^m = \sigma^m(a^m), \quad m=1,\ldots,L
Step 1: Base case (output layer): \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L} \odot \frac{dh^L}{da^L}
Step 2: Backward recursion for m = L-1, L-2, \ldots, 1: \begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} &= \underbrace{\left({W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}\right)}_{\text{from prev step}} \\
&\quad \odot \underbrace{\frac{dh^m}{da^m}}_{\text{known}}
\end{aligned}
Step 3: Weight gradients for all m: \begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} &= \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m}}_{\text{step 2}} \\
&\quad \cdot \underbrace{(h^{m-1})^\top}_{\text{forward pass}}
\end{aligned}
Gradient descent update: W^m \leftarrow W^m - \eta\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m}

Why is this efficient? A single forward pass (caching all a^m) plus a single backward pass gives all weight gradients simultaneously. Without caching, computing the gradient for layer 1 would require recomputing the same intermediate quantities over and over, far more expensive work that caching avoids at the cost of a little memory.


Connecting Back to Vanishing Gradients
In the backward recursion, each step multiplies by \frac{dh^m}{da^m}. For sigmoid, \max_x \frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{sigmoid}(x) = \frac{1}{4}. In an L-layer sigmoid network, the gradient reaching layer 1 is scaled by roughly \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^L, vanishing rapidly. For ReLU, the derivative in the active region is exactly 1 (no shrinkage). Toggle the “Tanh/Sigmoid + overlay derivatives” in the explorer above to see the saturation visually.






TipQuestion: How does this change when we train on a batch of examples instead of one?





With batching, each column represents one example. If the batch has B examples, every layer’s activations h^m become a matrix H^m of size N^m \times B, and column j holds the output of layer m for input example j. The batch size is the number of columns each layer outputs. The forward pass is the same computation applied to all columns at once:
A^m = W^m H^{m-1} + b^m \mathbf{1}^\top, \qquad H^m = \sigma^m(A^m)
Here \mathbf{1}^\top is a row of B ones, so the bias vector b^m is added to every column. The notes above write one example at a time with column vectors. Earlier, in the MLP section, we wrote H = XW_1, where each row of X is an example. The two conventions describe the same computation with rows and columns swapped.

Worked Example: One Forward and Backward Pass
The backpropagation section introduced a lot of notation at once. To see what each symbol does, we run one training step by hand on the smallest network that still shows every idea, using a batch of two examples so that the batch size shows up in the equations. The specific calculation a homework asks for is left to the assignment, and this example uses its own numbers.

Setup
The network has L = 2 layers with widths N^0 = 2, N^1 = 2, N^2 = 1. The hidden layer uses \sigma^1 = \operatorname{ReLU}. The output layer uses the identity, \sigma^2(a) = a, so h^2 = a^2. Each example has its own squared error \tfrac{1}{2}(h^2 - y)^2, and the loss \mathcal{L} is the average of these over the batch.
The batch has B = 2 examples. Each example is one column, so the input matrix X = H^0 is N^0 \times B = 2 \times 2 and the targets form a 1 \times B row Y:
X = H^0 = \begin{pmatrix} x^{(1)} & x^{(2)} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad Y = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
The starting parameters are:
W^1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad b^1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -0.5 \end{pmatrix}
W^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad b^2 = 0.5

So W^1_{21} is the weight from input unit 1 (column j = 1) into hidden unit 2 (row i = 2): the entry -1 in W^1. In a batch, the derivation’s single-example vectors gain a second index s. We write a^m_{ks} for the k-th pre-activation of example s, which is the entry in row k, column s of the matrix A^m. Likewise h^{m-1}_{js} is row j, column s of H^{m-1}.


Forward pass, and what gets cached
For each layer we compute A^m = W^m H^{m-1} + b^m \mathbf{1}^\top and then H^m = \sigma^m(A^m), where \mathbf{1}^\top is a row of B ones so that b^m is added to every column.






Note



Layer 1.
A^1 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ -0.5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad H^1 = \operatorname{ReLU}(A^1) = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}
Layer 2.
A^2 = H^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}
Loss. The per-example losses are \tfrac{1}{2}(2 - 1)^2 = 0.5 and \tfrac{1}{2}(-0.5 - 0)^2 = 0.125, so \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.5 + 0.125) = 0.3125.


Column 1 of each matrix is the single-input computation for x^{(1)}, for instance a^1_{\cdot 1} = (1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0,\; -1 \cdot 1 + 0.5 \cdot 2 - 0.5)^\top = (3, -0.5)^\top. Column 2 is the same computation for x^{(2)}. No column mixes with another, because each entry of W^m H^{m-1} combines one row of W^m with one column of H^{m-1}.
The forward pass caches (stores in memory) the matrices that backpropagation will need, instead of discarding them:







Cached value
Where the backward pass uses it




H^0 = X and H^1
the weight gradient \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^m}(H^{m-1})^\top


A^1
the ReLU derivative \frac{dh^1}{da^1}, which depends on the sign of each entry of A^1


H^2
the loss derivative \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^2}



Caching costs a little memory and saves recomputing any of these later. Without it, the gradient for layer 1 would need the forward pass through everything before it to be rerun.


What the chain-rule variable z_i is
In the chain rule section, z_1, \ldots, z_N were generic intermediate variables sitting between a parameter w and the loss \mathcal{L}. In an MLP, the variables we pivot through are the pre-activations a^m_k. So for a weight W^m_{ij}, the role of the z_k is played by a^m_k, and the sum in Step 1 of “Deriving the Weight Gradient” runs over k = 1, \ldots, N^m. Here N^1 = 2, so for a layer 1 weight that sum has two terms.


Backward pass
We work from the output back to the input, computing \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^m} at each layer (one column per example) and then the weight gradients from it.






Note



Base case, layer 2. The two pre-specified quantities are the loss derivative and the activation derivative. Because \mathcal{L} averages over the batch, the loss derivative carries a factor \frac{1}{B}:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial H^2} = \frac{1}{B}\,(H^2 - Y) = \tfrac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & -0.25 \end{pmatrix}
The identity has slope 1, so \frac{dh^2}{da^2} = 1 and
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^2} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & -0.25 \end{pmatrix}
Layer 2 gradients. Using the cached H^1, whose transpose is \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^2} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^2}\,(H^1)^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}
The bias gradient adds each example’s entry across the columns: \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b^2} = 0.5 + (-0.25) = 0.25.
Backward recursion to layer 1. Multiply by the transpose of the weights after layer 1, then by the ReLU derivative. The cached A^1 gives \frac{dh^1}{da^1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, since ReLU has slope 1 where A^1 > 0 and 0 where it is negative.
{W^2}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^2} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & -0.25 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 0.25 & -0.125 \\ -0.5 & 0.25 \end{pmatrix}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.25 & -0.125 \\ -0.5 & 0.25 \end{pmatrix} \odot \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 0.25 & -0.125 \\ 0 & 0.25 \end{pmatrix}
Layer 1 gradients. Using the cached input X = H^0, whose transpose is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^1} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^1}\,(H^0)^\top = \begin{pmatrix} 0.375 & 0.125 \\ -0.25 & 0.75 \end{pmatrix}
Summing each row of \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^1} across the columns gives \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b^1} = (0.125,\; 0.25)^\top.




Tracing one entry back through the derivation
The matrix formulas hide the indices, so we compute one entry the way “Deriving the Weight Gradient” does. Take m = 1, i = 2, j = 1, that is W^1_{21}. Its gradient should equal the (2,1) entry of the matrix above, -0.25.
Step 1 (chain rule through a^1_k). For one example s, the sum over k = 1, 2 has two terms:
\begin{aligned}
\text{contribution of example } s &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1_{1s}}\frac{\partial a^1_{1s}}{\partial W^1_{21}} \\
&\quad + \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1_{2s}}\frac{\partial a^1_{2s}}{\partial W^1_{21}}
\end{aligned}
Step 2 (which a^1_k contains W^1_{21}). The pre-activation a^1_{1s} is built from row 1 of W^1, so it does not contain W^1_{21} and its derivative is 0 (the k \neq i case). The pre-activation a^1_{2s} is built from row 2, so \frac{\partial a^1_{2s}}{\partial W^1_{21}} = h^0_{1s}, the value of input unit j = 1 for example s (the k = i case).
Step 3 (collapse the sum). Only k = i = 2 survives, so each example contributes \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1_{2s}}\, h^0_{1s}. The weight is shared by every example, so the batch adds these contributions over s:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^1_{21}} = \sum_{s=1}^{B} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1_{2s}}\, h^0_{1s} = 0 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot (-1) = -0.25
Here \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1_{2s}} is row 2 of \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^1}, which is (0, 0.25), and h^0_{1s} is row 1 of X, which is (1, -1). Step 4 is the observation that doing this sum for every (i, j) at once is the matrix product \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^1}(H^0)^\top: row i of the first factor times column j of the transpose adds over s. The result -0.25 matches the matrix computed above.
The same reading works for the output layer. For W^2_{11} (m = 2, i = 1, j = 1) we get 0.5 \cdot 3 + (-0.25) \cdot 2 = 1, the first entry of \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^2}.


Where the batch size appears

Shapes. Every H^m and A^m has B columns, N^m \times B. The parameters W^m and b^m have no batch dimension, since all examples share them.
The loss derivative. Averaging over the batch puts a factor \frac{1}{B} into \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial H^L}, and every later gradient inherits it.
The weight and bias gradients. The product \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^m}(H^{m-1})^\top sums over the B columns, which is the \sum_s above. The bias gradient is the plain sum over columns.
The recursion. {W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial A^{m+1}} and the Hadamard product act on each column independently, so examples do not mix on the way back either.



One gradient descent step
With learning rate \eta = 0.1, the update W^m \leftarrow W^m - \eta\,\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} (and likewise for b^m) gives
W^1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9625 & 0.9875 \\ -0.975 & 0.425 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad b^1 = \begin{pmatrix} -0.0125 \\ -0.525 \end{pmatrix}
W^2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4 & -0.95 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad b^2 = 0.475
Rerunning the forward pass on the same batch gives \mathcal{L} \approx 0.138, down from 0.3125. This is only a sanity check on a tiny smooth problem; in general \eta must be chosen with care (Week 1).






Tip





Check it yourself. A useful habit is to verify a hand-computed gradient numerically. Nudge one parameter by a small \epsilon, rerun the forward pass, and compare \frac{\mathcal{L}(W + \epsilon) - \mathcal{L}(W)}{\epsilon} with the backprop value. For W^1_{12} the backprop value is 0.125, and a nudge of \epsilon = 10^{-6} gives a change in loss very close to it.

title: Week 2: Multi-Layer Perceptrons & Backpropagation
text:
Summary






Note



Key takeaways from Week 2

Linear models cannot represent nonlinear relationships. Stacking affine layers collapses to a single affine map; depth buys nothing without nonlinearity.
Nonlinearity (an element-wise activation function \sigma) injected between linear layers gives the MLP its expressive power.
Sigmoid was the historical default; it suffers from vanishing gradients due to saturating derivatives. ReLU (gradient = 1 for x>0) avoids this and dominates modern practice.
Backpropagation is a three-step algorithm: (1) base case at the output layer, (2) backward recursion using the weight transpose, (3) outer product to get weight gradients. The forward pass caches activations to avoid recomputation.
The Universal Approximation Theorem guarantees a wide enough single-hidden-layer MLP can fit any function, but overfitting, model size, and the question of how to train are all open challenges.



Next lecture: Regularization and Overfitting - how to prevent the MLP from simply memorizing training data?

title: Week 3: Initialization, Autodiff, Overfitting & Regularization
text:
Backprop Revisited
Overview. Week 2 gave us the multi-layer perceptron and the backpropagation algorithm. This week asks what can go wrong when we actually train one, and what tools make training practical. We first restate backpropagation in Week 2’s notation and work one example end to end. That example shows why gradients can shrink or blow up as they travel backward, which motivates choosing the initial weights carefully. We then see how a program can apply the chain rule for us (automatic differentiation). Finally we turn from optimization to generalization: a model that fits its training data too well can do worse on new data, and two simple techniques, weight decay and dropout, push against that.
Week 2 already derived backpropagation. Here we restate it and use it in a worked example, keeping Week 2’s letters for the two quantities every layer computes.
With this notation the forward pass is a^m = W^m h^{m-1} + b^m and h^m = \sigma^m(a^m), where h^0 is the input \bm{x} and L is the last layer. Backpropagation (Backpropagation) then has three steps.
This step starts at the output layer: the loss depends on a^L only through h^L.
Here \odot is the Hadamard product, entry-by-entry multiplication. The gradient at layer m is built in two moves. First we multiply the gradient at layer m+1 by {W^{m+1}}^\top, the transpose of the weight matrix that carried layer m into layer m+1. Entry k of the result is \sum_\ell W^{m+1}_{\ell k}\,\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial a^{m+1}_\ell, so each unit in layer m collects the gradients of the units it fed, each weighted by the connection weight it used. We say the gradient is sent backward along the same connections that carried the activations forward. Second, we scale each entry by the local slope of the nonlinearity.
Once we know \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial a^m, the weight gradient is its outer product with the previous layer’s activations.

text:
Warning



Notation. These notes write the pre-activation of layer m as a^m and the activation as h^m, the same letters as Week 2. The handwritten slides for this lecture use z^m for the pre-activation and a^m for the activation, so a reader comparing the two should translate z \to a and a \to h.

\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial h^L}\,\frac{\partial h^L}{\partial a^L}



\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} &= \left({W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}\right) \odot \frac{\partial h^m}{\partial a^m}, \\
&\qquad m = L-1, \ldots, 1
\end{aligned}



\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^m} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m}\,{h^{m-1}}^\top



The cost of backpropagation
How expensive is one training step? Suppose the model is a stack of matrix multiplies and element-wise nonlinearities, and let |\theta| be the total number of parameters (all weights and biases). A matrix multiply does one multiply-add per entry of the weight matrix, and a weight matrix has far more entries than its layer has units. The matrix multiplies therefore dominate the cost, and the nonlinearities add comparatively little. For a single example, the forward pass costs roughly |\theta| multiply-adds.
The backward pass has two parts, and each costs about as much as the forward pass:

The recursion multiplies by {W^{m+1}}^\top at every layer. That is a matrix–vector product with the same number of entries as the forward multiply.
The weight gradients are outer products. Each produces an object as large as W^m itself.

Note



Rule of thumb. One training step (forward plus backward) costs roughly three forward passes, about 3|\theta| multiply-adds per example. This is why training compute is often estimated directly from the parameter count.




Worked example: sigmoid units with cross-entropy loss
Take a network for binary classification where every layer, including the output layer, uses the sigmoid function:
h^m = \operatorname{sigmoid}(a^m) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp(-a^m)} \qquad \text{for all } m, \text{ including } m = L
The label is y \in \{0, 1\}, and the loss is the cross-entropy from Week 1, written here for a single output:
\mathcal{L}(\bm{x}, h^L) = (y - 1)\log(1 - h^L) - y \log(h^L)
Output layer. The two factors in the first step are the derivative of the cross-entropy and the derivative of the sigmoid. The sigmoid’s derivative can be written using its own output, \partial h^L / \partial a^L = h^L(1 - h^L). Then:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^L} = \frac{h^L - y}{h^L(1 - h^L)} \cdot h^L(1 - h^L) = h^L - y
The denominator of the cross-entropy derivative cancels exactly against the sigmoid derivative, leaving the prediction minus the label. This is the same “\hat{\bm{y}} - \bm{y}” form we saw for softmax and cross-entropy in Week 1.
One layer back. Apply the recursion with m = L-1. The local slope is again the sigmoid derivative, now evaluated at layer L-1:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{L-1}} = \left({W^{L}}^\top (h^L - y)\right) \odot h^{L-1}\left(1 - h^{L-1}\right)
Weight gradient. The gradient for the weights of layer L-1 multiplies this by the activations of layer L-2:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^{L-1}} = \left({W^{L}}^\top (h^L - y)\right) \odot h^{L-1}\left(1 - h^{L-1}\right)\, {h^{L-2}}^\top
Reading the result from left to right, the error h^L - y is multiplied by {W^L}^\top, which sends it backward along the connections into layer L-1, and then each entry is multiplied by a sigmoid slope factor h^{L-1}(1 - h^{L-1}). Every additional layer we go back adds one more such pair of factors. That repeated pattern is the subject of the next section.






TipQuestion: What does one more layer back look like, with actual numbers?





Apply the recursion once more, with m = L-2. The gradient at layer L-1 is multiplied by {W^{L-1}}^\top, which sends it backward along the connections into layer L-2, and each entry is then scaled by the sigmoid slope of layer L-2:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{L-2}} = \left({W^{L-1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{L-1}}\right) \odot h^{L-2}\left(1 - h^{L-2}\right)
Substituting the previous line shows the pile-up. The result contains two matrix factors and two slope factors, in the order they were met going backward:
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{L-2}} &= \left({W^{L-1}}^\top \left[\left({W^{L}}^\top (h^L - y)\right) \right.\right. \\
&\qquad \left.\left. \odot\, h^{L-1}(1 - h^{L-1})\right]\right) \odot h^{L-2}(1 - h^{L-2})
\end{aligned}
To see how fast this shrinks, use the smallest possible network: one unit per layer, so every quantity is a single number, with every weight equal to 1. Suppose each unit sits at a = 0, so every activation is h = 1/2 and every sigmoid slope is h(1 - h) = 1/4. Take y = 1. Then the output error is h^L - y = 1/2 - 1 = -1/2. Multiplying by a weight of 1 leaves a number unchanged, so each step back only multiplies by the slope 1/4:

Each layer back divides the signal by 4, so after three layers it is 1/64 of its size at the output. This is the best case for the sigmoid, since 1/4 is the largest slope it can have, and it assumed weights of 1 that neither shrink nor grow the signal. Since no larger slope is available, only the weights could offset the shrinkage, which is why the initialization section below focuses on them.

title: Week 3: Initialization, Autodiff, Overfitting & Regularization
text:
Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
How do the gradients of early layers behave in a deep network? Look again at the recursion:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^m} = \left({W^{m+1}}^\top \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^{m+1}}\right) \odot \frac{\partial h^m}{\partial a^m}
Going back one layer applies two operations, and each is repeated at every layer:

Repeated matrix multiplies. The factor {W^{m+1}}^\top appears once per layer. Multiplying a vector by many matrices can shrink it toward zero or grow it without bound, depending on the size of the weights.
Repeated nonlinearity derivatives. The factor \partial h^m / \partial a^m also appears once per layer.







TipQuestion: Why can multiplying by weight matrices again and again make the gradient explode or vanish?





Start with one number. Multiplying by 2 three times turns 1 into 8, and multiplying by 1/2 three times turns 1 into 1/8. A matrix behaves the same way along special directions. An eigenvector of a matrix M is a direction \bm{v} that M only stretches or shrinks, M\bm{v} = \lambda\bm{v}, and the number \lambda is its eigenvalue. Applying M a total of k times to \bm{v} gives \lambda^k \bm{v}, which grows when |\lambda| > 1 and shrinks when |\lambda| < 1.
For example, let M stretch the first coordinate by 2 and shrink the second by 1/2. Applying it three times to (1, 1)^\top gives
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/2 \end{pmatrix}^{3} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 8 \\ 1/8 \end{pmatrix}
The first entry exploded and the second vanished.
In the backward recursion the matrix is different at every layer, so no single eigenvalue decides the outcome. What matters is how much each matrix tends to stretch or shrink the vectors passing through it. If they tend to stretch, gradients explode. If they tend to shrink, gradients vanish. These matrices are the weights themselves, so their scale is something we control through how we initialize them.



For the sigmoid, this second factor is at most 1/4. The sigmoid equals 1/2 at a = 0 and flattens toward 0 and 1 on either side, so its slope is largest at 0, where it equals 1/4, and falls toward 0 for large |a|.

Figure 1. Both panels share the same vertical scale (dashed line at 1). The sigmoid rises from 0 to 1. Its slope never exceeds 1/4, and it is close to 0 whenever the input is far from 0.


Definition. Vanishing gradients occur when the gradient shrinks toward 0 as it is propagated backward, so that early layers receive almost no learning signal. Exploding gradients occur when it grows toward \infty instead. See the vanishing gradient problem.

Both come from the same recursion. If the repeated factors are typically smaller than 1 in size, the gradient decays layer by layer; if they are typically larger, it grows. In a sigmoid network the slope factor alone contributes at most 1/4 per layer, which is why Week 2 already flagged vanishing gradients for sigmoid.






Warning



Why sigmoid is rarely used as a hidden activation. The ReLU activation from Week 2, \operatorname{ReLU}(a) = \max(0, a), has a derivative that is exactly 0 or exactly 1. Where it is 1, multiplying by it over and over neither shrinks nor grows the gradient. This is one reason ReLU made much deeper networks practical to train.


The slope factor is fixed once we choose the activation function. The weight factor is not: it is set by how we choose the weight matrices before training even starts. That is the next topic.

title: Week 3: Initialization, Autodiff, Overfitting & Regularization
text:
Parameter Initialization
Before training starts, every weight needs a value. The slides use the word initialize to mean something specific: choose a probability distribution and sample the initial weights from it. If we want to avoid vanishing and exploding gradients, the choice of that distribution matters, and the variance of the weights is the natural knob.

Definition. Parameter initialization is the choice of the distribution from which the initial values of the model’s weights are sampled before training begins.


Two bad ideas
Why not start with every weight equal to 0? Then W\bm{x} = \bm{0} for every input, so each layer’s output stops depending on the input at all (ignoring the bias). Training cannot easily fix this either. The backward recursion multiplies by {W^{m+1}}^\top = 0, so at initialization every layer below the output receives exactly zero gradient, and even after updates begin, the units within a layer stay identical to each other.






TipQuestion: What does starting from all zeros look like, with actual numbers?





Take the smallest network that shows both effects: input \bm{x} = (1, 2)^\top, a hidden layer of two sigmoid units, and one output unit with no nonlinearity, so h^2 = a^2. The loss is \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}(h^2 - y)^2 with target y = 1, and the learning rate is \eta = 0.1. Every weight and bias starts at 0.
Step 1, forward. The hidden pre-activations are a^1 = W^1\bm{x} + b^1 = (0, 0)^\top. The sigmoid of 0 is 1/2, so h^1 = (0.5, 0.5)^\top. The output is a^2 = W^2 h^1 + b^2 = 0, so h^2 = 0.
Step 1, backward. At the output, \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial a^2 = h^2 - y = -1. The output weights get a real gradient, because they multiply the nonzero activations h^1:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^2} = (-1)\,(0.5,\; 0.5) = (-0.5,\; -0.5), \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial b^2} = -1
The hidden layer gets nothing, because the recursion multiplies by {W^2}^\top = (0, 0)^\top. The sigmoid slope at 0 is 1/4, but a slope times zero is still zero:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1} = \left({W^2}^\top(-1)\right) \odot \tfrac{1}{4} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
Since the weight gradient is \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial a^1 times \bm{x}^\top, it is zero too:
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W^1} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
Step 1, update. Only the output layer moves: W^2 = (0.05,\; 0.05) and b^2 = 0.1. The hidden weights W^1 and biases b^1 are still all 0.
Step 2. The hidden layer is unchanged, so h^1 = (0.5, 0.5)^\top again, and the output is now a^2 = 0.05 \cdot 0.5 + 0.05 \cdot 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.15. Then \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial a^2 = 0.15 - 1 = -0.85, and the hidden layer finally receives a nonzero gradient, because W^2 is no longer zero:
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial a^1} &= \begin{pmatrix} 0.05 \\ 0.05 \end{pmatrix}(-0.85) \odot \tfrac{1}{4} \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} -0.010625 \\ -0.010625 \end{pmatrix}
\end{aligned}
Both hidden units receive the same number. The weight gradient multiplies this by \bm{x}^\top = (1, 2), so both rows of \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial W^1 equal (-0.010625,\; -0.02125), and the update gives
W^1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.0010625 & 0.002125 \\ 0.0010625 & 0.002125 \end{pmatrix}
The two rows, and the two entries of b^1, are identical. Two units with identical weights and biases compute identical outputs, so they receive identical gradients on every later step and stay identical forever. The hidden layer of two units behaves as a hidden layer of one, which is the wasted capacity described above.
The specific numbers here are our own, invented for illustration, not from the lecture or a homework. In this sigmoid network the zero hidden gradient lasts only one step. The identical-units problem does not go away.



Why not give every weight the same nonzero constant, say 1? Then every row of W computes the same dot product with the input, so every hidden unit computes the same function. We waste nearly all of the layer’s capacity on redundant copies. We need initial values that are random but carefully scaled, and the scale is what the next subsections work out.


A variance refresher
The derivation below uses three facts about a random variable X. The variance is \operatorname{Var}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2, which reduces to \mathbb{E}[X^2] when \mathbb{E}[X] = 0. The normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, s^2) has mean 0 and variance s^2. For independent variables, the expectation of a product is the product of expectations, \mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\,\mathbb{E}[Y].






TipQuestion: Can these three facts be checked on actual numbers before we use them?





Take a random variable X that equals -1 or 1, each with probability 1/2. Its mean is \mathbb{E}[X] = \tfrac{1}{2}(-1) + \tfrac{1}{2}(1) = 0, and \mathbb{E}[X^2] = \tfrac{1}{2}(-1)^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}(1)^2 = 1. Since the mean is 0, the variance is just \mathbb{E}[X^2]:
\operatorname{Var}[X] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 = 1 - 0^2 = 1
This matches a \mathcal{N}(0, 1) variable, which by definition has variance 1.
Now take a second variable W, independent of X, equal to -2 or 2, each with probability 1/2. By the same computation, \mathbb{E}[W] = 0 and \operatorname{Var}[W] = \mathbb{E}[W^2] = 4, matching a \mathcal{N}(0, 4) variable, so its \sigma^2 = 4.
To check \mathbb{E}[WX] = \mathbb{E}[W]\,\mathbb{E}[X], list all four equally likely combinations of (W, X) and their products:



W

Averaging the last column, \mathbb{E}[WX] = \tfrac{1}{4}(2 - 2 - 2 + 2) = 0, and indeed \mathbb{E}[W]\,\mathbb{E}[X] = 0 \cdot 0 = 0. The two sides agree because every value of W pairs with both values of X equally often, so the positive and negative products cancel. This is the same cancellation used below to drop the cross terms W_{ij}x_jW_{ik}x_k with j \neq k: the sum has both signs of each factor appearing equally often, so its average is 0.





Variance of one linear layer
Consider a single linear layer with no nonlinearity, mapping an input \bm{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_\text{in}} to an output \bm{h} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_\text{out}}:
\bm{h} = W\bm{x}, \qquad h_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n_\text{in}} W_{ij}\, x_j
The slides make three assumptions: there is no nonlinearity, each input entry satisfies x_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), and each weight satisfies W_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), all independent. The question is what \sigma to use.
Because every W_{ij} and x_j has mean 0 and they are independent, \mathbb{E}[h_i] = 0. So the variance of h_i is just \mathbb{E}[h_i^2]. Expanding the square of the sum produces cross terms of the form W_{ij}x_j W_{ik}x_k with j \neq k; each has expectation 0 by independence and zero mean, so only the squared terms remain:
\operatorname{Var}[h_i] = \mathbb{E}[h_i^2] = \sum_{j=1}^{n_\text{in}} \mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^2\, x_j^2]
Independence splits each expectation, and \mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^2] = \sigma^2 and \mathbb{E}[x_j^2] = 1:






TipQuestion: Where do the values E[W_ij^2] = sigma^2 and E[x_j^2] = 1 come from?





Both follow from the identity in the variance refresher above, \mathbb{E}[X^2] = (\mathbb{E}[X])^2 + \operatorname{Var}[X], applied to a mean-0 variable, where the first term vanishes and \mathbb{E}[X^2] reduces to \operatorname{Var}[X].
W_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) by assumption, so \mathbb{E}[W_{ij}] = 0 and \operatorname{Var}[W_{ij}] = \sigma^2. Then \mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^2] = 0^2 + \sigma^2 = \sigma^2.
Likewise x_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), so \mathbb{E}[x_j] = 0 and \operatorname{Var}[x_j] = 1, giving \mathbb{E}[x_j^2] = 0^2 + 1 = 1.
Neither value takes any work beyond reading off the variance of the assumed distribution, because the assumed mean is 0 in both cases.



\operatorname{Var}[h_i] = \sum_{j=1}^{n_\text{in}} \mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^2]\,\mathbb{E}[x_j^2] = n_\text{in}\,\sigma^2
The output has variance n_\text{in}\sigma^2 while the input has variance 1, so the layer multiplies the variance by n_\text{in}\sigma^2. Stack many layers and this factor is applied repeatedly: if it is above 1 activations grow with depth, if below 1 they shrink.


Choosing sigma
Forward pass. To keep the variance of the activations near 1, we want n_\text{in}\,\sigma^2 = 1.
Backward pass. In the backward pass the roles of input and output swap, because the gradient is multiplied by W^\top and each entry of the result is a sum over n_\text{out} terms. The slides therefore state the analogous requirement n_\text{out}\,\sigma^2 = 1 (the lecture gives this by analogy and does not repeat the derivation).
Unless n_\text{in} = n_\text{out} the two requirements disagree. The slides settle on a compromise, averaging them:
\frac{n_\text{in}\,\sigma^2 + n_\text{out}\,\sigma^2}{2} = 1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{2}{n_\text{in} + n_\text{out}}}

W_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\; \frac{2}{n_\text{in} + n_\text{out}}\right)

This is called Xavier or Glorot initialization (see weight initialization). It keeps the layer’s variance factor near 1 in both directions when the layer widths differ, without being exact for either. The derivation also assumed no nonlinearity, so for a network with activation functions it is a starting heuristic and not a guarantee.






Note



He initialization. If we instead assume a ReLU activation, the same style of derivation gives a slightly different scale, \sigma = \sqrt{2/n_\text{in}}, called He initialization. The lecture states this result without the derivation. One intuition, which is ours and not from the slides: for zero-mean, symmetric pre-activations, ReLU sets roughly half of them to 0, which halves the average squared activation, and the extra factor of 2 compensates. Most deep learning frameworks default to one of Xavier or He initialization. Homework 3 assumes ReLU, so the He scale is the relevant one there; the specific calculation is left to the assignment.

title: Week 3: Initialization, Autodiff, Overfitting & Regularization
text:
Automatic Differentiation
Backpropagation for an MLP took a page of matrix calculus. Can a program produce gradients for any model we write, without us deriving them by hand? The answer is yes, and the tool is called automatic differentiation, or autodiff (in PyTorch, autograd). See automatic differentiation.

A small running example
The slides use a tiny network with one hidden unit. We treat every quantity as a single number, so that the chain of operations is easy to see:
h = \operatorname{ReLU}(w_h x + b_h), \qquad o = w_o h + b_o, \qquad \mathcal{L} = (y - o)^2
The subscripts h and o name which layer a quantity belongs to, hidden or output, not an index running over several units: w_h and b_h are the hidden layer’s weight and bias, and w_o and b_o are the output layer’s. The same convention carries into the computational-graph diagram below, where the intermediate results m_h, a_h, and m_o take the subscript of whichever layer’s computation produced them.
Here \operatorname{ReLU}(a) = \max(0, a) as in Week 2. The parameters are w_h, b_h, w_o, b_o, and we want the four gradients \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_o, \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial b_o, \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_h, and \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial b_h. Here h is the single hidden unit’s output, the one-number version of the activation h^m above, and o is the network output.


Break the computation into single operations
We can always use the chain rule. To make that mechanical, first rewrite the forward computation as a sequence of single simple operations, giving each intermediate result a name:
\begin{aligned}
m_h &= w_h x, & a_h &= m_h + b_h, & h &= \operatorname{ReLU}(a_h), \\
m_o &= w_o h, & o &= m_o + b_o, & e &= y - o, \\
\mathcal{L} &= e^2
\end{aligned}
Then the gradient with respect to w_h is a product of one derivative per operation on the path from \mathcal{L} back to w_h:
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_h} &= \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial e}\,\frac{\partial e}{\partial o}\,\frac{\partial o}{\partial m_o} \\
&\quad \cdot \frac{\partial m_o}{\partial h}\,\frac{\partial h}{\partial a_h} \\
&\quad \cdot \frac{\partial a_h}{\partial m_h}\,\frac{\partial m_h}{\partial w_h}
\end{aligned}
Each factor is the derivative of one elementary operation, and each is simple:







Operation
Derivative used




\mathcal{L} = e^2
\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial e = 2e


e = y - o
\partial e/\partial o = -1


o = m_o + b_o
\partial o/\partial m_o = 1


m_o = w_o h
\partial m_o/\partial h = w_o


h = \operatorname{ReLU}(a_h)
\partial h/\partial a_h = 1 if a_h > 0, else 0


a_h = m_h + b_h
\partial a_h/\partial m_h = 1


m_h = w_h x
\partial m_h/\partial w_h = x



Multiplying them gives \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_h = 2e \cdot (-1) \cdot w_o \cdot \mathbb{1}[a_h > 0] \cdot x, where \mathbb{1}[a_h > 0] is 1 when a_h > 0 and 0 otherwise.


What autodiff needs to do
To compute any one gradient, such as \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_h, we need to know two things:

Which operations were applied, and in what order.
The derivative of each operation.

So an autodiff system does three jobs:

It defines a set of operations.
It defines the derivative of each of those operations.
It keeps track of which operations were applied, in a computational graph.


Definition. A computational graph records a computation as a graph. Each node is either an input (a leaf node, such as x, y, or a parameter) or the result of one operation applied to earlier nodes. The graph is built as the forward computation runs.

Figure 2. The computational graph of the small network. Arrows show the direction values flow in the forward computation. Operations run up the left column, ending at the loss L. Leaf nodes (inputs and parameters) hang off to the right, and x sits at the bottom. The highlighted path from L to w_h is the one whose local derivatives are multiplied to give the gradient of L with respect to w_h.

To compute \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w_h, find the path in the graph between \mathcal{L} and w_h and multiply the derivatives of the operations along it. That product is exactly the chain-rule product above, so autodiff is backpropagation applied to an arbitrary graph of operations instead of only to a stack of layers. The forward values that some of the derivatives need, such as x or a_h, are the intermediate results the graph has already recorded.






TipQuestion: Why does the exponent 2 get its own node in the graph?





The slides draw the loss \mathcal{L} = e^2 as a “pow” operation with two inputs: e, and a separate leaf holding the number 2. That follows from how an autodiff library defines its operations.
One power operation, not one per exponent. Rather than having separate “square”, “cube”, and so on, the library defines a single power operation, \operatorname{pow}(u, k) = u^k, that works for any exponent. The exponent is then an input to the operation, the same way w_o and h are the two inputs to the multiply that forms m_o. Every input to an operation is a node in the graph, so the exponent appears as a node too.
It is a leaf because nothing computes it. Leaf nodes are the values the computation starts from. The constant 2 is not produced by any earlier operation, so it sits at the edge of the graph alongside x, y, and the parameters.
The backward pass needs its value. The backward rule for power is \partial u^k/\partial u = k\,u^{k-1}. To apply it at the loss node, the library must know k, and it reads the inputs of an operation from the nodes the graph recorded, just as the multiply rule reads h to compute \partial m_o/\partial w_o = h. With k = 2 the rule gives 2e, which is the \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial e in the table above.
No gradient is needed for it. The 2 is not a parameter we train, so, like x and y, we never use a gradient with respect to it.
This is a design choice, not a law. A library that had a dedicated “square” operation with a single input would have no node for the 2. That is why a question that asks you to count nodes states the convention up front, for example “raise to a constant power (the exponent is a separate leaf node)”.



Putting the pieces together gives the general procedure:

Automatic Differentiation
Define, once, for a small library of elementary operations (add, multiply, subtract, power, ReLU, and so on):

forward: how to compute the operation’s output from its inputs.
backward: the derivative of the output with respect to each input.

Given a model (a composition of these operations):

Forward pass. Evaluate every operation in order, and record which operations were applied to which inputs. This record is the computational graph.
Backward pass. Start from \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathcal{L} = 1. Visit the nodes in reverse topological order, meaning each node only after every node that uses it. At each operation node, multiply the node’s accumulated gradient by the operation’s derivative with respect to each input, and add the result to that input’s running gradient.

When the sweep finishes, every leaf node holds its gradient. One sweep gives the gradients for all leaves at once.

The word add matters. If a node feeds into more than one later operation, there is more than one path from the loss to it, and the chain rule says to sum the contributions of the paths (the “multiple intermediate variables” case in Week 2). Adding each contribution into a running total performs that sum without listing the paths. For example, in m = w \cdot w the leaf w is both inputs of one multiplication. If the gradient arriving at m is g, the backward rule sends g\,w to each of the two inputs, and adding them gives 2gw, which matches the derivative of w^2.
The course’s Homework 3 has you build this machinery yourself. These notes explain the idea, and the implementation is left to the assignment.
